 America needs Canada’s aluminum. Trump’s tariff exposed just how badly.
 Ryan Dezember , The Wall Street Journal 10 min read 27 Oct 2026, 06:41 AM IST 
 Summary
 Smelters in Quebec run on cheap hydroelectric power. The Trump administration’s 50% tariff has pushed up prices for American industry. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 SAGUENAY, Quebec—When Nazi planes were blitzing London during World War II and the U.S. needed to build more aircraft and munitions in a hurry, it helped turn this remote place in the Canadian forest into an aluminum-production juggernaut.
 Thousands of Canadians labored through frigid conditions to build smelting pots and a hydropower plant to fuel them—in just 18 months. Ever since then, Saguenay’s aluminum plants have supplied American industry.
 Now, President Trump’s trade war has cast Canada’s aluminum smelters as the enemy—and U.S. businesses and consumers are paying a price.
 During his first term, Trump exempted Canada from a 10% aluminum tariff that he imposed on other trading partners. After he returned to the White House, he stripped Canada of its exemption and raised the tariff rate on aluminum to 50%.
 “They’ve treated the United States very unfairly,” Trump said last month about Canada. “They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world.” He has said the U.S. has no need for Canada’s natural resources.
 Aluminum has emerged as one of the trade war’s biggest conundrums. The steep tariff—imposed in the name of national defense—is intended to stimulate U.S. production. Yet the enormous power requirements for making aluminum have meant that Canada, where abundant hydropower has kept electricity prices from rising as sharply as in the U.S., has supplied about 70% of U.S. aluminum imports in recent years.
 The tariff has pushed aluminum prices in the U.S. to a record premium over global benchmarks, punishing home buyers, data-center developers, automakers and grocery shoppers. In addition to the new levy, trading restrictions on Russian metal and the Iran War, which choked off Persian Gulf exports, have contributed to global price increases.
 In Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney is turning to Europe to forge new trade partnerships. The European Union’s top official said last month that she would work to add Canada as the trade bloc’s first associate member. Trump responded by threatening further tariffs on Europe and calling Canada “a terrible trade partner.”
 Alcoa, which dominated American aluminum production for decades, built the facilities upstream from the Saguenay Fjord, expanded them during World War II, then spun them off to meet antitrust rules. The hydropower stations, smelters, ore docks and other facilities are owned now by Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto.
 Rio, one of the largest aluminum producers outside China, is starting up in Saguenay the West’s first new smelters in more than a decade. The company also is working in Quebec to commercialize a new carbon-free smelting process in a joint venture with Alcoa and the provincial government, with support from the Canadian government and Apple.
 Much of the Canadian aluminum entering the U.S. comes from Rio’s Saguenay operation, which ships about 70% of its output across the border.
 “We always call aluminum ‘solid electricity,’” said Jérôme Pécresse, who runs Rio’s aluminum, lithium and Canadian businesses. “We cannot find a source of power in the U.S. which is anywhere close to what we have in Canada in terms of competitiveness.”
 In the U.S., Trump’s push for domestic smelting has met resistance.
 Emirates Global Aluminium, the Mideast’s largest producer, and Chicago-based Century Aluminum have said they would spend more than $4 billion to build what would be the largest U.S. smelter, capable of more than doubling domestic production of primary aluminum. The Biden administration awarded $500 million for the project, and Trump has thrown his support behind it with additional incentives.
 But opposition to the project has swelled in Inola, the Oklahoma prairie town chosen as the site. Local critics have expressed concerns about pollution and foreign ownership of land and objected to taxpayer-funded incentives to the developers.
 After a rowdy, marathon meeting in June where Trump officials promoting the smelter were heckled and booed, the Inola town council placed a moratorium on building permits and entitlements in its industrial park. Owners of property near the site sued in federal court seeking to block construction.
 The smelter became a divisive issue in Oklahoma’s Republican gubernatorial primary. Former state senator Mike Mazzei came out in favor of it and won Trump’s endorsement and the nomination. But he faced xenophobic political ads aimed at the project’s Mideast investors.
 “Mazzei wants to give your tax dollars to a Muslim country to build a smelter,” said the narrator in an ad made by a group called Put Oklahoma 1st. “Foreign workers, foreign landownership, threatening our way of life.”
 On a public call to rally support for Mazzei, Trump vouched for Emirates Global—“very fine people with unlimited money”—and said the smelter would bring jobs, tax revenue and the envy of other states.
 “This country desperately needs aluminum,” he said. “We get it all from Canada, for the most part, and we need it badly.”
 American empire
 During the 20th century, the U.S. led the world in aluminum production.
 In 1886, Charles Martin Hall, a 22-year-old working in the woodshed behind his parents’ home in Oberlin, Ohio, had figured out how to mass produce it inexpensively using electric currents. Until then, aluminum had been so difficult to separate from its ore that it was more expensive than gold
 The Hall-Héroult production process—named for the Ohioan and a young Frenchman who simultaneously made the discovery—ushered in new eras in aviation, electronics, const

docs.title: Fell for a fake trading app or guaranteed-return WhatsApp group? What to do immediately? Can you recover your money?
docs.text:
WhatsApp and Telegram groups are often used to build a false sense of trust through fake profit screenshots and stock tips, before members are directed to fraudulent trading apps that can drain their savings. According to data from Ministry of Finance, as many as 235 lakh of demat accounts were added during FY 2026 (till December 2025), pushing the total count beyond 21.6 crore. The mutual fund industry also continued to expand, with 5.9 crore unique investors recorded at the same period, of which 3.5 crore (as of November 2025) were from non-tier-I and tier-II cities. The rising scams prompted the Securities and Exchange Board of India ( Sebi ) to issue an advisory warning investors against WhatsApp stock-tip groups that use fraudulent tactics to create a false impression of credibility and lure investors. In a statement on Thursday, the market regulator said that certain unregistered persons were offering stock recommendations to investors through invitation-only WhatsApp groups under the guise of free investor education. These operators often use overseas numbers posing as market experts. "To make these calls look credible, certain members, acting in concert with the operators, post false claims of profit and praise the 'expert'. This practice, known as astroturfing, creates a false impression of genuine support and induces unsuspecting investors to act on the call," Sebi said. If you already fell for a fake trading app or guaranteed-return WhatsApp group and lost money, recovery may be possible if you act quickly. According to a blog post by Tata Mutual Fund , a fraud victim should immediately contact their bank or payment provider, call the national cybercrime helpline at 1930, and lodge a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. Prompt reporting can improve the chances of blocking or tracing the funds before they are withdrawn or transferred further, although recovery is not guaranteed. However, you cannot force a refund or sue a broker or company just because a stock recommendation or tip went bad. This is why consulting a Sebi-registered investment advisor can be a prudent approach for making investments. In January last year, Sebi introduced restrictions on how finfluencers can provide stock-related content under the guise of investor education on social media. Stock prices used for educational purposes must be at least three months old, and live stock prices cannot be used. Registered entities are also prohibited from paying influencers for any direct or indirect association'. Here are some more tips, as per the blog post, that may help you avoid fake apps and WhatsApp investment scams in India: — Treat ‘guaranteed return’ claims as a warning sign: Markets are volatile and mostly unpredictable in nature, so anyone promising you guaranteed returns or saying that they could double or triple your investment money in short time must be treated as a potential scam. Remember that as per Sebi guidelines, legitimate investment platforms and apps cannot promise assured returns. — Stay away from investment advice shared on WhatsApp groups: Scammers often use WhatsApp to pose as market experts and run guaranteed return scams in India. Be wary of the links shared on WhatsApp groups as these links can be phishing scams that can empty your bank account. — Always verify credentials Don’t take investment advice from individuals or platforms without verifying their registration status as only Sebi-registered investment advisers can offer investment advice to clients. — Check if the app is legitimate: Before you start investing through a trading or investment app, check if they have Sebi's ‘verified’ badge on your phone's app store. You can also go to the investor support page on Sebi's website and check the list of Sebi-authorised intermediary apps. Disclaimer: This story is for educational purposes only. The views and recommendations made above are those of individual analysts or broking companies, and not of Mint. We advise investors to check with certified experts before making any investment decisions. Eshita Gain is a digital journalist at Mint, where she joined in May 2025. While her core beat lies in business and finance, she is not confined to a single niche and frequently explores stories across domains, including international relations and policy developments.

She holds a postgraduate diploma in business and financial journalism by Bloomberg from the Asian College of Journalism (ACJ), Chennai. During her time there, she received rigorous training in tracking financial data, interpreting corporate filings, and reporting on business developments. She has pursued her graduation from St. Joseph’s University, Bengaluru in a multi-disciplinary course. Her majors included Journalism, International Relations, peace and conflict studies.

Eshita has previously worked in digital marketing, which enables her to write SEO friendly copies that are clear and engaging.

Her primary interest lies in breaking down complex subjects and writing clear, accessible copies that inform readers. She aims to bridge the gap between technical financial language and everyday understanding. docs.title: The Yes Bank AT1 bond case and lessons for all investors
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 The Yes Bank AT1 bond case and lessons for all investors
 Joydeep Sen 4 min read 26 Oct 2026, 01:46 PM IST 
 Summary
 Investors must look through the recent returns and packaging of a product, understand the risks and invest only if it suits their risk appetite. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The contours of the Yes Bank Additional Tier 1 case are now known to all investors. The entire quantum of ₹ 8,415 crore was written off. 
 Aggrieved investors moved the Bombay high court, which overturned the decision to write it off. This decision was challenged in the Supreme Court, which upheld the order of the Bombay high court. Now the issue is about the pending coupon (interest). 
 Measure from Sebi 
 The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) took some measures as a fallout of the write-off of Yes Bank’s AT1 bonds in March 2020. On 6 October 2020, Sebi notified that only qualified institutional buyers would be allowed to participate in the issuance of AT1 instruments. The circular stated that the minimum allotment of AT1 instruments should not be less than ₹ 1 crore and the minimum trading lot size for AT1 instruments should be ₹ 1 crore. 
 Effectively, individuals were pushed out of the AT1 market, and rightfully so. There are certain risk aspects of AT1 bonds , which individual investors may or may not comprehend.
 Lessons for investors 
 The issue that the aggrieved investors raised at the Bombay high court was that the product was mis-sold to them. AT1 bonds have certain risk factors that were not communicated to them and are now known, in hindsight. 
 These were sold as something “similar to fixed deposits” of the same bank but yielding higher returns. From a generic standpoint—not about the AT1 issue in particular—mis-selling is an issue. However, the investor would do well to be careful and adopt the adage of caveat emptor , or buyer beware. Let us look at certain broad thumb rules. 
 Returns come from risk: If financial investment product A is expected to give returns higher than product B, then there is a higher risk in A. This is not to say you should not invest in product A but do so only after understanding the risks. It should suit your risk appetite. 
 Bonds are available with yields of 8 percent, 10 percent, 12 percent and 14 percent. You have to pick and choose the one that matches your risk appetite. 
 When we look at charts of year-wise returns from various investment products, for the highest number of years, the winner has been Bitcoin. This is something that does not have a solid base for investing in it and the investor has to be careful. 
 Look through the packaging: Since financial investment products do not have a physical look and feel to it, it is packaged and sold with certain features. An actively managed fund may outperform the relevant benchmark, which is the selling plank. But you never know. 
 If the fund underperforms the benchmark, you will incur the management expenses, anyway. A sectoral or thematic fund may give returns higher than the large cap benchmark, but investors tend to invest at the peak of the cycle. 
 Unit-linked insurance plans ( Ulips ) package investment with insurance with a bundle of illiquidity and expenses. The investor should compare standalone investment avenues with the bundled offering of Ulips. Now that the regulator has proposed a reduction in expenses, the industry is fighting back – time for investors to take a stand that they are not mere bystanders.
 Ask the right questions: If the question to the financial adviser/product seller is kitna dega (how much return would it yield?) then you will not get the answer to the basic question of why that product is suitable for you. You would have heard the Sebi-mandated tagline umpteen times: past performance may or may not be sustained in the future. However, bonds have a stated yield when you invest in them. 
 In the context of AT1 bonds, there is no need to brush the entire category with the same brush. There are public sector banks with implied support of the government. There are leading private sector banks, which are flagships of the banking system. 
 The segment of AT1 bonds is now meant for institutional investors and the minimum ticket size is ₹ 1 crore. There are high-yielding products available in the market for high net worth individuals, such as portfolio management schemes and alternative investment funds, which come with a minimum ticket size of ₹ 50 lakh and ₹ 1 crore, respectively. 
 There are performing credit or private credit funds that have portfolio yields in double digits. This will be a diversified portfolio , rather than putting ₹ 1 crore in one bond.
 From a broader perspective, the investor has to look through the recent returns and packaging of the product, understand the risks and invest only if it suits their risk appetite. 
 Joydeep Sen is a corporate trainer (financial markets) and author.

Mint Money 
 Rupee down, US yields up: Is it time to add Treasuries to your portfolio?
 Ananya Grover 5 min read 26 Oct 2026, 07:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 Rising US Treasury yields and a weaker rupee are drawing Indian investors toward dollar-denominated debt as a fixed-income diversifier. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Mumbai: The surge in US Treasury yields, with the 10-year touching 5.37% earlier this month, its highest since 2002, is opening another avenue for Indian investors to access the world’s largest economy. With the rupee weakening and the gap between US and Indian bond yields narrowing, experts advise considering US debt to diversify fixed-income portfolios.
 Global bond yields have been rising amid a surge in crude oil and other commodity prices, driven by the West Asia war. That is stoking inflation concerns and prompting a shift towards tighter monetary policy. The gap between 10-year US and Indian government bond yields has narrowed to around 2 percentage points. The shrinking differential is adding to the appeal of dollar-denominated debt, particularly as the rupee has depreciated 8.38% against the dollar over the 12 months to 23 October.
 Nirav Karkera, head of research and fund manager at W by Groww, said interest in US debt is building amid high US yields and a weaker rupee. Indian mutual funds investing in US Treasuries manage only about ₹ 400 crore, largely because most have stopped accepting fresh investments due to the industry’s overseas investment limits, he said.
 Nirav Karkera, head of research and fund manager at W by Groww, said interest in US debt is building amid high US yields and a weaker rupee. Indian mutual funds investing in US Treasuries manage only about ₹ 400 crore, largely because most have stopped accepting fresh investments due to the industry’s overseas investment limits, he said.
 A weaker rupee can boost returns in rupee terms. For instance, a 4-5% return in dollars on short-term US Treasuries could translate into 7.5-8% in rupee terms, before fees and taxes, assuming annual rupee depreciation of 2.5-3%.
 One alternative is to invest through the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), which allows Indian residents to remit up to $250,000 a year for permitted transactions. At Vested Finance, a global investment platform that gives Indian retail investors access to international financial markets, around 5% of investors have invested in US debt, said Viram Shah, the company’s founder and chief executive. Here is a closer look at the available routes and the considerations for investors.
 Different routes
 One option is to invest through an Indian mutual fund scheme that invests in US Treasuries or other overseas debt securities. Investors can transact in rupees without opening an overseas brokerage account, while the fund handles the investments. However, most such schemes have stopped accepting fresh subscriptions because of the industry’s overseas investment limits: $7 billion for overseas mutual fund investments and a separate $1 billion limit for overseas exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Those limits are already exhausted.
 “The more practical route today is LRS, which allows individuals to remit up to $250,000 a year for eligible overseas investments, including US Treasury securities and US-listed Treasury ETFs, while accounting for foreign-exchange conversion costs and tax collected at source (TCS),” said Karkera.
 Investors can access overseas-listed products, such as the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF, iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF and Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF, through platforms such as INDmoney and Vested Finance, subject to product availability. While this route offers a wider choice of investments, investors must factor in foreign-exchange conversion costs, brokerage charges and tax-compliance requirements, and be comfortable managing an overseas investment account.
 “GIFT City could become a convenient route for US debt as more products offering exposure to US debt are launched,” Karkera said.
 Tax considerations
 Indian debt funds purchased on or after 1 April 2023 no longer qualify for long-term capital gains treatment and are taxed at the investor’s applicable income-tax slab rate, irrespective of the holding period. Gains on US-domiciled debt ETFs, however, are subject to a different tax treatment, with long-term capital gains taxed at 12.5%.
 Shah said the tax treatment of ETFs holding US bonds depends on the product and remains unsettled in some cases. Indian tax authorities and financial experts continue to debate whether these funds should be taxed as foreign assets or as debt funds. “Tax should not be the main reason to move money into US debt,” Shah said.
 The rupee is an important determinant of returns, Shah said. A weaker rupee boosts returns in rupee terms, as it has over the past year, while a recovery in the currency can erode them. “US debt is a currency decision as much as a rate decision,” he said, adding that diversification is a stronger reason to consider US debt, given that most Indian investors hold nearly all their fixed-income assets in rupees.
 A small dollar allocation could make sense for investors who expect to spend money overseas in the next few years, such as on education or travel, Shah said. He also advised investors to favour shorter-maturity Treasuries. Longer-dated bonds are more vulnerable to price declines if yields rise further, while shorter maturities carry less interest-rate risk.
 The US-10 year yield has eased since early October, and was at 4.97% down from an early October peak of 5.37%.

 Eleven hours of Trump: what we saw on the ground at seven rallies in seven days
 Philip Wegmann , Natalie Andrews , Alex Leary , The Wall Street Journal 8 min read 26 Oct 2026, 06:55 AM IST 
 Summary
 The blitz of visits to largely red states aims to stem GOP losses by motivating Trump supporters to show up on Election Day. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Joe Douglas knew what to expect when he drove 90 minutes to see President Trump in Wichita, Kan., this week. “I’ve heard everything he is going to say,” the 70-year-old retired pipeline worker said, sporting the red MAGA hat he bought in 2016.
 So why make the drive? “Because this is live,” Douglas said Monday, adding that he had never seen the president, whom he voted for in the past three elections, in person.
 Trump has returned to the rally stage in force, hoping to energize his supporters and defy the polls predicting deep Republican losses in November. Crowds are generally smaller than they were when he was on the ballot, but the president is reveling in the attention, touting his agenda, stirring the pot and veering off script.
 President Trump headlined seven campaign rallies in a week, hoping to boost voter turnout for the midterm elections. Photo: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters
 Some Republicans fear the spectacle will motivate Democrats and give his opponents plenty of fodder to paint the president as out of touch. But at the arenas, gyms and airport hangars where he has been holding court, the Trump show is unabashedly back—perhaps for a final time as his decadelong dominance in politics begins to sunset.
 Wall Street Journal reporters attended every one of Trump’s midterm rallies this week: seven events across seven states, starting in Kansas on Monday and ending in Michigan on Sunday, with stops along the way in North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa, Florida and Georgia. All told, Trump spoke for more than 11 hours. By Saturday, his voice was noticeably hoarse.
 Here’s what we learned:
 All about Trump
 The rallies are something of a security blanket for Trump, according to advisers, freeing him from the pressures of the job, critical news coverage and the lowest approval rating of any president heading into midterm elections in Wall Street Journal polling dating to the 1990s. Most analysts expect the GOP will lose control of the House and possibly the Senate.
 But on stage, Trump is met with cheering crowds and fleeting signs of opposition. In Sioux City, Iowa, congressional candidate Joe Mitchell lamented Trump hasn’t been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize and presented him with a framed “man of the century” certificate. Trump pauses at rallies to play a video clip of a CNN analyst explaining that among Republican voters, he is far more popular than Ronald Reagan or Abraham Lincoln.
 Throughout the week, Trump addressed critics who allege that he is slipping by returning to one of his favorite topics: the mental acuity test that he says he aced: “I know everything that I’m doing,” he told a crowd in South Carolina.
 Trump also said no fewer than 10 times in Wichita that “nobody appreciates me” despite what he considers his many accomplishments, a routine that culminated in a story he told about expressing that sentiment to a group of businessmen at the White House. “And then I look up and I say, ‘Oh, wait…is this the Oval Office that we’re in?…That means I’m president.”
 Few things annoy Trump more than a small crowd. Friday in Fort Myers, Fla., he marveled at a packed arena on a college campus and claimed the crowd outside was “10 miles long.” There were a large number of people outside, but the line didn’t stretch for 10 miles. At every rally he points out how many cameras are in the back of the room. “Oh, wow, that’s a lot of fake news,” he said in North Carolina to laughter and boos.
 A midterms strategy
 Critics see self-aggrandizement, a blizzard of falsehoods and increasingly uncivil attacks on his opponents. But there is a strategy behind putting Trump at the center of the midterms. Advisers see Trump as the single best motivator for voters.
 The Trump political machine is rerunning much of the playbook that returned him to the Oval Office in 2024: targeting the MAGA base, especially low-propensity voters, in red states. A senior White House official said that despite Trump’s polarizing nature, the approach is paying dividends, pointing to Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has seen an uptick in enthusiasm in internal metrics.
 Still, it is a risky approach. Far-reaching Republican losses in the midterms could signal that Trump’s political power is diminishing. And the president has made statements at his rallies that could make life harder for vulnerable Republicans.
 Saturday night in Georgia, Trump bragged that oil revenues in the U.S. are surging because of the conflict in the Middle East. He said that his advisers told him not to say that because people are paying more for gasoline. “But I said, ‘I don’t give a damn, I’m gonna say it: We’re making a freaking fortune.’ Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are gonna come down,” Trump said.
 Some longtime political allies wonder if the grueling pace is getting to the 80-year-old president. Mike Lindell, a businessman and longtime friend of the president’s, said during a recent videoconference with Trump’s allies that the president “looked the tiredest I’ve ever seen him.” Lindell added, “You’ve got to realize, these rallies are just one after another after another.”
 A White House official said nonstop travel has pushed the administration to its limits, but insisted that Trump is energized. After rallies, the president has asked aides which part of his remarks they liked best, according to people involved in the conversations.

 Indian IT companies see business in policing AI agents
 Jas Bardia 4 min read 26 Oct 2026, 09:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 Tata Consultancy Services, Cognizant, HCLTech, and Tech Mahindra have each stated that managing AI agents and governing their use are emerging as new business opportunities 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Companies that raced to unleash artificial intelligence (AI) agents to book meetings, fix code and pitch clients autonomously are now scrambling to keep them in check, amid fears that these digital workers could go rogue or access data well beyond their remit.
 And India’s largest information technology (IT) services firms are lining up to sell them policing software. Tata Consultancy Services Ltd, Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp., HCL Technologies Ltd, and Tech Mahindra Ltd have each stated that managing AI agents and governing their use are emerging as new business opportunities.
 While India’s largest IT services firm, TCS, and fifth-largest Tech Mahindra are doubling down on software to coordinate AI agents and govern their limits, third-largest HCLTech is acquiring firms to strengthen its capabilities in managing these agents. Cognizant, meanwhile, has launched its own offering to govern AI usage.
 Disciplining AI agents
 On 8 October, TCS’s management stated that “strong AI governance with secure AI platforms is becoming a top need for enterprises”.
 “I think as the enterprises are focused on safe, secure, and responsible deployment of agentic AI , they need a strong foundation to scale. So, building the AI platform, and more so this year, the agentic control plane is becoming a key layer not just in terms of governance, but in terms of cost management, really looking at agent performance and the full end-to-end agent lifecycle,” said Aarthi Subramanian, chief operating officer, during TCS's post-earnings analyst call.
 “Agents inherit the access rights of the application or the human who deployed them, they operate in silos tied to a single vendor 's platform, and the controls that stop two agents from duplicating work or reaching into data they should never see are mostly manual,” said Phil Fersht, chief executive of HFS Research.
 Nasdaq-listed Cognizant launched its own software layer to manage AI on 23 October. It launched Cognizant AI Nexus, which measures AI spend, governs AI output quality and documents results across teams.
 It also gave a sneak peek at the ways it governs AI use. Nexus captures the best IT processes and turns them into templates that teams and AI agents can reuse. Because the same system tracks both spending and quality, companies can see whether their AI is getting cheaper, better and faster. As part of this offering, each AI agent gets its own ID, permissions and memory, and the company decides what it can access. Every task is logged, and humans still sign off on important decisions and compliance checks.
 While Cognizant built its own, HCLTech acquired a firm to strengthen its AI management capabilities. On 28 September, it announced its intent to acquire Croatia-based software firm Robotiq.ai to strengthen orchestration across AI agents and enterprise applications.
 The rise of automation further complicates the kinds of data these agents can access. Tech Mahindra’s management addressed “heightened concerns about security and reliability of AI agents”.
 “Trust is fundamental to scaling AI. Responsible AI is embedded throughout the solution lifecycle, with red teaming, trusted data, traceability, security, and IP provenance built into how we design, deploy, and operate AI solutions,” said Atul Soneja, COO, during its 15 October post-earnings analyst call.
 TCS, HCLTech, and Tech Mahindra ended the September quarter with $7.64 billion, $3.72 billion, and $1.69 billion in revenue. Cognizant is expected to announce its September quarter results on 29 October.
 Growth area
 The rise of AI governance tools could also be attributed to the need to complete tasks assigned to an agent.
 “Orchestration is the next significant opportunity because the concept of agentic AI has moved beyond isolated AI deployments. Just as teams need to work together to drive meaningful output, orchestrating agents to work together to complete a task is important. This will help in end-to-end scale implementations,” said Namratha Dharshan, chief business leader for India research at Information Services Group.
 She added that homegrown tech services firms are well-poised to meet demand because of their process, domain, and industry knowledge.
 Both Fersht and Dharshan expect orchestration to be a growth opportunity in the near future.
 “This is a constantly evolving field and not a one-time activity. As more agents enter the system, continuous monitoring and improvement will be critical, and these platforms will be highly integrated into enterprise environments and tools to provide real-time monitoring and visibility for the organization. Especially in a highly regulated environment, this will become even more critical,” said Dharshan.
 Fersht said that “for Indian IT firms, the test is whether they can move from reselling a hyperscaler's orchestration stack to owning a point of view on how an enterprise should govern intelligence across its whole estate, which means investing in forward-deployed talent, in proprietary harness IP and in commercial models tied to measurable outcomes rather than headcount”.

docs.title: The long shadow of ‘zombie firms’ on India Inc, in charts
docs.text:
Plain Facts 
 The long shadow of ‘zombie firms’ on India Inc, in charts
 howindialives.com 6 min read 26 Oct 2026, 10:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 After peaking during the pandemic, the share of listed ‘zombie firms’—companies that don’t generate enough profits to service their debt—has been sliding. But the stock of accumulated financial stress has been fairly high to make a big difference. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 What binds telecom major Vodafone, infrastructure company IVRCL, Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar Ltd and real estate company Unitech? For each of them, profit before interest and taxes was insufficient to cover interest payments for three consecutive years up to 2024-25. Effectively, they were either defaulting on their loans or borrowing more or raising capital to service them.
 In finance parlance, such companies are called ‘zombie firms’. They keep going, but their fragility limits their own prospects and, at a broader level, those of the overall economy. A recent study by Dun and Bradstreet (D&B) shows that while their absolute numbers remain significant, their relative prevalence has declined from six years ago. Yet, it remains high enough to cast a shadow over the economy.
 Debt management 
 This D&B study, released in September, assessed around 6,000 listed Indian companies between 2015 and 2025 on the ‘interest coverage ratio’ (ICR). Mathematically, this is the profit before interest and taxes divided by the interest payable. An ICR figure above 1 means the company has sufficient surplus to service its interest obligations; below 1 means it doesn’t. The study classified firms with an ICR below 1 for a given year as ‘stressed’ and for three straight years as a ‘zombie’.
 Sufficient data was available for 81% of the 6,000 companies. During the annual period from 2017 to 2025, the share of observable firms classified as either stressed or zombie was the highest when the covid pandemic resulted in hard lockdowns—23.5% in 2020 and 22.2% in 2021. In 2025, this figure dropped to 14.2%—the lowest during the study period amid an improvement in the broader corporate environment, according to D&B. 
 Half recovery 
 There are companies that have spent several years in the stressed or zombie sets. For example, IVRCL has had an ICR below 1 since 2014-15 at least, and Unitech since 2015-16. But there are also companies, even with solid businesses, that enter this set only to exit it later. For example, telecom major Bharti Airtel had an ICR below 1 from 2018-19 to 2020-21, resulting in its classification as a zombie in 2020-21. However, it has since become healthier and pulled itself out. Conversely, its rival Vodafone has lingered there since 2018-19.
 The D&B study shows that, on average, one among five listed companies acquired zombie status at least once between 2015 and 2025. In other words, it’s a common business occurrence. The larger question is what happens to them once they enter that set. Of the 971 companies that were classified as zombies in any year between 2015 and 2025, about 43% had made a full (over 1 ICR for two consecutive years) or temporary recovery (over 1 ICR for one year) in 2025. But about 25% of the set retained its zombie status in 2025, while another 10% were stressed. 
 Sectors in stress 
 Given that companies compete for common resources, it’s more efficient for an economy to see a dynamic reallocation of resources from weak firms to strong firms with high growth potential. According to the D&B study, this landscape appeared considerably healthier, although it also reflected stronger debt-servicing capacity rather than direct evidence of efficient capital allocation. 
 “At the same time, declining zombie prevalence does not immediately eliminate the existing stock of financial stress, as firms that enter prolonged distress can take considerably longer to recover,” it added. 
 There are some sectors where the incidence of zombie companies is higher, suggestive of fundamental shifts. A howindialives.com analysis of ICR of listed companies for a three-year period from 2022-23 to 2024-25 with more than ₹ 10 crore interest payout (translating into roughly ₹ 100 crore debt) shows that construction and textiles had the highest number of such firms. However, as a share of all companies in each sector, stress was more pronounced in cement, telecom and media. 
 Asian comparison 
 While the D&B report examines the share of stressed and zombie companies among listed Indian firms, a September working paper by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), covering listed and unlisted companies across 10 prominent Asian economies from 2005 to 2021, found that India had a high prevalence of zombie firms.
 Zombie firms accounted for 16% of Indian companies (second highest in this set) and 14.2% of Indian corporate assets (third highest). The BIS paper traces a significant increase in the share of zombie firms across the 10 economies—from 11% in 2008 to 17% in 2021 by number of firms and 6% to 13% by assets.
 To be sure, the period and criterion used by the two papers differ slightly. Both the D&B study and the BIS paper used the same base criteria—ICR of below 1 for three straight years. However, D&B is based only on listed companies, while BIS included both listed and unlisted firms. Moreover, BIS used stricter criteria for removing the zombie tag. BIS demands three consecutive years of ICR above 1 to remove the zombie tag as against D&B that requires two years. 
 Next-order effects 
 The BIS paper identified “evergreening practices by weak banks” as a key reason for this asymmetry across the Asian economies . In simpler words, instead of writing off a loan, let’s say of ₹ 100 crore, a weakly capitalized bank lends the company another ₹ 10 crore to service the loan and keeps it going.

docs.title: Personal loan closed but credit score not improving? Experts explain why
docs.text:
Closing a loan reduces overall debt and eases the stress of owing money, but its impact on a credit profile depends on several factors, including how quickly credit bureaus update their records, repayment history and overall credit utilisation. Understanding these basics can help borrowers manage their credit profiles better and build a stronger financial record over time.
 Loan closures are not reflected in credit reports instantly. Lenders generally share account updates with credit bureaus periodically, so borrowers may have to wait several weeks before the loan is marked as ‘closed’.
Raj P. Narayanam, Founder & Executive Chairman, Zaggle, explained: “Closing a personal loan is a financial milestone, but the score does not respond instantly. Lenders report to the bureaus on a monthly cycle, so the closure can take 30 to 45 days to be reflected. Once the loan closes, you also lose an active account that was contributing to your credit mix . The good news is that a closed loan with a clean repayment record stays on your report and keeps supporting your history.”
 He further stated, "To keep the score moving upward, maintain an active credit card with regular usage and timely payments, such as zagg.money.” It is important to note that zagg.money is Zaggle's consumer payments and credit card platform. 
 Shakti Shekhawat, Business Head at BharatLoan, touched on what a borrower should do after closing a loan. He stated that “Closing a personal loan does not guarantee an immediate improvement in your credit score , as credit bureaus may take time to update the loan status in their records. A borrower’s credit profile also depends on repayment history, outstanding balances and overall credit utilisation. Consistently meeting payment obligations and maintaining a healthy credit mix can help strengthen creditworthiness over time.” 
 Therefore, borrowers should check their current credit score and credit report after the lender's reporting cycle is complete to ensure that the loan is marked as ‘closed’ or ‘settled’ in their case, and to confirm that no pending dues remain on the outstanding amount. 
 Staying vigilant is the key to proper financial management . It is also important to note that if the status is marked incorrectly, the borrower should promptly contact the lending institution and dispute it with the relevant credit bureau to resolve the issue amicably. 
 Closing a personal loan is a positive step towards becoming debt-free, but score updates can take time, and a score reflects overall financial behaviour rather than a single transaction. Paying all dues on time, keeping the credit utilisation ratio under control and checking credit reports regularly for errors are simple steps that help maintain a healthy credit profile.

docs.title: Special intensive revision: What's the road ahead for the Election Commission of India?
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Special intensive revision: What's the road ahead for the Election Commission of India?
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 26 Oct 2026, 07:31 AM IST 
 Summary
 The special revision of electoral rolls has seen several issues that left voters out of the draft rolls and raises questions about the process. Here's why India needs more transparency from the Election Commission. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 During the British Raj, only the wealthy and the educated enjoyed the right to vote. After India won freedom, one of the first tasks of the leadership was to expand the electoral rolls to include all eligible adults. This was a formidable task as Partition refugees were still streaming into the country, princely states were yet to be integrated, and the rules of citizenship weren’t finalized by the constituent assembly. 
 Despite stiff odds, independent India’s first draft electoral roll was ready even before the Constitution had been enacted. A small team of civil servants ensured that even the most marginalized inhabitants found a place in the list of voters. 
 When Bengali refugees from what was East Pakistan then complained that they did not have any documents required, the rules were relaxed for them, historian Ornit Shani wrote in How India Became Democratic . The inclusive and empathetic nature of India’s electoral processes , uncommon in the world then, ensured its legitimacy, Shani noted. 
 In contrast, the exclusionary nature of the latest Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls has caused a legitimacy crisis for the election commission today. 
 This revision may have begun with the right intentions. An accurate up-to-date list of voters can help check electoral malpractices and make elections representative. 
 But in their zeal to eliminate wrong entries, election officials seem to have gone overboard, denying many voters the right to vote. In West Bengal, many voters found their way back to the voter list only after the elections were over, and after months of bureaucratic paperwork. The process became a test of how badly a citizen wanted to keep her right to vote. 
 It doesn’t take much to imagine the choice an economically weak citizen would make if made to pick between earning daily wages and getting back on the electoral rolls. 
 Not just opposition leaders, some of the government’s most vocal supporters—including a former economic advisor to the prime minister—have raised complaints about being left out of the draft rolls. In Congress-ruled Karnataka, members of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) staged protests against the Commission. 
 After The Indian Express reported that two of the three election commissioners had raised objections about the SIR process, the commission relaxed some of its rules. A 26 September press note said that the updated rules were approved by “the full Commission.” It did not state whether all the SIR rules and changes in voter registration forms had been approved by the full Commission or not. 
 There is no evidence to suggest that the exclusion of legitimate voters favoured the BJP in the Bihar and Bengal elections. But that in itself does not diminish the shortcomings in the process. It was poor and women voters who faced the brunt, since they lacked documents to satisfy an intransigent bureaucracy. 
 India’s political class must strive to re-establish the legitimacy of one of India’s most storied institutions. Rules of appointments to the commission and the manner in which it functions today need to change. 
 The 2023 law that tilted powers towards the government of the day to select election commissioners needs to be revisited. The commission must be independent, and seen to be so. The government needs to reach out to the Opposition and frame a national consensus. The long lever of nation building rests on a fulcrum called negotiation.

She holds a Bachelors in Mass Media (BMM) and Post Graduate Diploma (PGD) in Journalism and Communication and has previously written for online business and markets news site Moneycontrol (Network18), Business-to-business (B2B) trade publications — the industry magazines Power Today and Solar Today (ASAPP Media), and the national news agency United News of India (UNI).
Outside of work, Jocelyn keeps up-to-date with local and international news, enjoys reading fiction books, novels and short stories, and enjoys movies, travelling and art.

Global 
 The biggest takeaways from Anthropic’s IPO prospectus
 Corrie Driebusch , Kate Clark , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 27 Oct 2026, 06:48 AM IST 
 Summary
 From the potential to cure cancer and a huge cushion of cash to humans losing control of AI models, here’s what stood out in Anthropic’s S-1 filing. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Anthropic has officially started the clock on what could be the biggest initial public offering ever. The maker of Claude unveiled its IPO paperwork Monday morning, putting it on track to go public as soon as the week before Thanksgiving.
 The 400-page prospectus offered a mix of promise and peril. Artificial intelligence, it said, could usher in a new era of progress, transforming how people code, conduct research, build financial models and automate routine tasks, and even help cure major diseases like cancer. At the same time, AI could lead to the development of new bioweapons, “destabilize the geopolitical order” and evolve beyond the ability of “humans to understand and control.”
 The paperwork offers the most detailed look yet at the AI giant’s gigantic ambitions, eye-popping finances and tightly controlled structure. Investors will be poring over it in the coming days, ahead of Anthropic’s so-called roadshow, roughly two weeks from now, when the company will pitch them on the roughly $100 billion in shares it hopes to sell.
 Anthropic revealed it plans to trade on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker “ANT.” Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley landed the most coveted underwriter roles among the more than 20 banks involved. While Anthropic remained tight-lipped about its targeted valuation, people familiar with the matter expect it to land between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.
 Massive loss and growing revenues
 Anthropic’s revenue jumped 1,300% from a year ago, with the company reporting $16.3 billion in the six months ended June 30, up from $1.2 billion in the year-earlier period.
 But it also disclosed an $80.7 billion net loss for the first half of the year, a figure that largely reflects an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements. Its expenses included almost $9 billion in compute and infrastructure spend, up from $2.3 billion in the same period last year and more than all of the $7.3 billion the company recorded for all of 2025.
 Its operating loss, which measures the profitability of its core operations, was much smaller: $693 million, down from $2.1 billion a year earlier.
 For all the talk about how much money AI loses, Anthropic has a lot of it. The company said that it had $112.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30. That is 80% of the $141.1 billion it has raised in the six years since its founding. Anthropic also had $19.3 billion of short-term investments in a variety of securities, including money-market funds.
 Anthropic has maintained a strong balance sheet thanks to rapid revenue growth and improvements in its use of computing power, the company said in its filing. It even managed to eke out a small operating profit in the second quarter—a stark contrast to its biggest rival OpenAI, whose losses deepened.
 A $40 trillion opportunity and immense risk
 Anthropic didn’t explicitly list a “total addressable market” figure—a business term for potential revenue opportunities—but effectively suggested it was $40 trillion. That tops the record-breaking $28.5 trillion TAM Elon Musk’s SpaceX highlighted in its IPO earlier this year.
 Anthropic arrived at its figure by estimating the economic value globally in 2025 performed by “knowledge workers.” The Journal had previously reported Anthropic was expected to estimate a number north of $30 trillion for the work that can be done with AI models.
 On the flip side, around 94 pages of the filing was dedicated to risk factors, including the possibility of misaligned models causing real-world harm. Anthropic said AI models can show “self-preserving” qualities to avoid being shut down and can generate responses that resemble “blackmail” in an effort to persuade humans to allow them to continue operating.
 Anthropic said it has taken steps in its terms of service to limit its liability for its models’ actions, but warned it could still be liable in some cases. Anthropic added that “the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident” might be so large that it would be unable to obtain insurance to cover the potential damages.
 Unconventional governance
 Anthropic’s capital structure essentially cuts regular shareholders out of most company decisions.
 The company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust will have the power to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, through its control of the sole share of Anthropic’s Class T stock.
 Meanwhile, Anthropic’s founders are also among its largest disclosed individual shareholders, including Dario and Daniela Amodei, Jack Clark, Tom Brown, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah. Each holds more than 200 million shares.
 The company’s founders will have the power to appoint the remaining directors and determine most or all other shareholder votes through control of a single Class F share with precisely 50.1% of voting power “with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally.”
 That share will be held by a closely held company called Founder LLC, tying together Chief Executive Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and five other founders, the filing said. Each of the seven will have equal say on wielding the founders’ vote in Anthropic decisions.
 A share class, dubbed Class E, will later go to employees other than co-founders, with only limited voting rights. None of these special share classes have economic rights, meaning a claim on the company’s underlying value.
 Soaring infrastructure costs
 Anthropic is on the hook to pay more than $475 billion in compute capacity agreements ove

Recipe for spotting multibaggers: Research, patience & a dash of luck
 Contrarian bets on capacity expansion, generational change in management, and corporate turnarounds can create opportunities for outsized returns, said experts.
 Puneet Wadha, editor, markets (left); Ambareesh Baliga, independent market analyst (middle); and U R Bhat, co-founder & director, Alphaniti Fintech (right)
 Puneet Wadhwa Saloni Goel Mumbai | New Delhi 7 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 11:50 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Spotting a multibagger is rarely straightforward. A company that eventually delivers several times its original share price may, at the outset, look no different from one that struggles to survive. Identifying the eventual winners requires fundamental research, patience, and a bit of luck, experts said at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit's Smart Investor Arena in Mumbai on Monday.
 “You cannot say on day one that a stock is a multibagger. Multibaggers evolve,” said Ambareesh Baliga, independent market analyst, during a discussion with Puneet Wadhwa on Hunting for Multibaggers: Skill, Luck or Patience?
 According to U R Bhat, co-founder and director of Alphaniti Fintech, identifying potential multibaggers requires investors to look beyond short-term share price movements and assess a company's underlying business prospects. Contrarian thinking, added Baliga, management quality, and the ability to execute growth plans are equally important, while investors must remain patient enough to allow their investment thesis to play out.
 But without luck, Baliga believes, it is difficult to reach that goal of finding a multibagger. "Luck plays a part, no doubt. It is a universal truth," he said.
 However, he observed that one cannot expect to be rewarded if they don't put in the hard work. "Do your hard work, analyse the company, and continuously track it. And hard work does not only mean labour; it also means the application of the mind. If that is in place, along with possibly some luck, you could have a multibagger," Baliga.

 Bhat identified three key drivers of a company's value: revenue growth, margins, and asset intensity.
 “The company has to keep growing its top line. Second, it needs good margins, and preferably improving margins. Third is asset intensity. The company has to generate sales and better margins with as little investment as possible,” he said.
 A sufficiently large addressable market, a differentiated product or service, and the ability to capture market share are also essential considerations.
 These factors form the foundation of fundamental research. Investors must determine whether a company has the potential to achieve them, based on the information available at the time of investment.
 However, strong fundamentals alone do not guarantee that a stock will become a multibagger, experts said. At an early stage, the characteristics of a company that eventually succeeds may not be dramatically different from those of one that fails. The difference often becomes apparent only over time, as management's ability to execute its plans determines the business's trajectory.
 Bhat said investors must conduct thorough research before investing and continue monitoring a company's performance thereafter. "Capacity expansion, generational change and corporate turnarounds can also create opportunities for outsized returns. However, these opportunities require patience, rigorous research and the discipline to track business fundamentals rather than react to short-term market noise," Bhat said.
 Earnings growth
 Share prices are influenced by both earnings growth and changes in the price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings.
 Bhat argued that while earnings growth can generate attractive returns, dramatic multibagger gains often require a significant expansion in the valuation multiple.
 A company that grows its earnings by 15-30 per cent annually for a limited period may deliver good returns, but such growth alone may not necessarily make it a multibagger. A substantial re-rating can amplify the gains, particularly when market perceptions of the business change.
 This re-rating may be driven by factors beyond the company's immediate operations. Changes in the macroeconomic environment, the emergence of a new market, or a shift in investor sentiment can alter how the market values a business.
 Contrarian investing
 Contrarian investing, too, Baliga said, can help investors identify such opportunities early.
 His approach involves looking for companies or sectors that have fallen out of favour and are trading at a discount to their potential. If business performance subsequently improves and the market begins recognising the opportunity, investor interest can build.
 As the company continues to deliver, the initial recovery can turn into broader market enthusiasm, potentially leading to a sharp expansion in its valuation multiple.
 However, the process is far from assured. A company may recover sufficiently to deliver a decent return without becoming a multibagger.
 Baliga cited examples of cyclical sectors such as steel and sugar, which have moved in and out of favour over time. Buying when sentiment is depressed and selling when it recovers can be profitable, but such a cycle does not necessarily produce the fundamental transformation required for a multibagger.
 The more significant opportunities arise when the underlying business or its prospects change materially.

FSN E-commerce Ventures (NYKAA): ADD CMP: ₹330 FV: ₹370 Resistance: ₹335/345 Support: ₹320/313 FSN E-commerce Ventures (NYKAA) is India's leading omnichannel beauty, personal care, and fashion retailer, supported by a strong consumer franchise, differentiated omnichannel presence, and a growing portfolio of owned brands. The company is well-positioned to capitalize on structural tailwinds from rising discretionary consumption, increasing online penetration, premiumization, and growing demand for beauty and personal care products. Strong Q2FY27 business momentum: Nykaa reported a robust Q2FY27 business update, with broad-based growth across both Beauty & Personal Care (BPC) and Fashion segments. The update highlights resilient consumer demand and reinforces the company's healthy growth trajectory ahead of the festive season. Continued market share gains, strong customer engagement, and expansion across categories remain key growth drivers. Compelling growth outlook: We expect Nykaa to deliver a healthy ~27 per cent revenue CAGR over FY26-29E, led by sustained momentum in the BPC business, rapid Fashion scale-up, category expansion, premiumization trends, and increasing contribution from owned brands. The BPC segment, Nykaa's core business, is expected to maintain its leadership position and deliver ~27 per cent revenue CAGR during FY26-29E, supported by strong brand partnerships and favorable industry dynamics. Earnings growth to outpace revenue growth: Beyond strong top-line expansion, Nykaa is entering a phase of improving profitability. Higher operating leverage, better fulfillment efficiencies, moderation in customer acquisition costs, and a growing mix of owned brands are expected to drive margin expansion. Consequently, we estimate a ~90 per cent PAT CAGR over FY26-29E, significantly outpacing revenue growth and underscoring the scalability of the business model. We believe Nykaa offers an attractive combination of category leadership, strong execution, multiple growth levers, and improving profitability. With Beauty continuing to compound strongly and Fashion gradually scaling up, the company remains well-positioned to create long-term shareholder value. We remain positive on the stock and maintain our ADD rating, with a revised DCF-based fair value of ₹370 per share. Muted asset quality outlook likely to weigh on Shriram Finance stock
 Shriram Finance shares may remain under pressure as rising credit costs, monsoon-related stress and a weaker asset quality outlook offset strong Q2 earnings and NII growth.
 premium 
 Shriram Finance reported a 60% rise in Q2FY27 net profit to ₹3,680 crore, but higher credit costs and asset quality concerns weighed on investor sentiment.
 Devangshu Datta New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 11:19 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Shriram Finance reported mixed numbers in the July-September quarter of 2026-27 (Q2 FY27). It is likely to miss the previous guidance on credit costs and asset quality deterioration is a serious concern. The management believes that high credit costs will continue through the second half of FY27 but estimates this is a temporary, near-term issue.
 While the market reacted negatively selling the stock lower (down over 8 per cent to ₹823.50 apiece post results), some analysts pointed to strong net interest income (NII) growth, net interest margin (NIM) expansions, good pre-provision operating profit (PPOP) returns and assets under management (AUM) growth. AUM growth projections and guidances are moderate and may be exceeded.
 An erratic monsoon and continuing stresses caused by the West Asia war are among the root causes for stress. Weak monsoons led to higher slippage and hike in credit cost guidance. 
 Among India’s leading non-bank lenders, Shriram Finance’s Q2FY27 profit after tax (PAT) rose 60 per cent year-on-year (Y-o-Y) to ₹3,680 crore and NII grew 40 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹8,410 crore. Other income grew 15 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹420 crore. The cost-to-income (C/I) ratio dipped 290 basis points (bps) quarter-on-quarter (Q-o-Q) to 22.9 per cent. The company’s guidance is that the C/I ratio will normalise at 25 per cent and operating expenses/AUM will be around 2.5 per cent over the long term.
 The PPoP grew 53 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹6,810 crore. Credit costs hit ₹1,880 crore, annualising at credit costs of 2.35 per cent compared to 1.9 per cent each in Q1FY27 and FY26. The FY27 AUM growth guidance was reset at a band of 15-17 per cent from 18 per cent earlier. 
 Disbursements grew 25 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹54,100 crore in Q2FY27 with AUM up 4.9 per cent Q-o-Q and up 17 per cent Y-o-Y at ₹3.29 trillion. Growth was driven by commercial vehicles (CV), passenger vehicles (PV), gold loans and personal loans, but growth in farm equipment, and two-wheelers (2W) was weak. Disbursement growth was supported by expansion to create an all-India footprint in the micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) segment.
 Shriram Finance is cautious in projections across drought-affected Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana. Management cautioned credit costs could rise temporarily by 30-40 bps over the next one or two quarters due to seasonal stress in affected geographies, but there is a ceiling of 2.3 per cent for FY27 which will not be exceeded.
 The asset quality outlook is cautious. Analysts are assuming higher credit costs alongside higher NIM and lower operating expenses. AUM and PAT could grow by high teens and over 30 per cent, respectively, over FY26-28, with return on asset (RoA) at 4.1 per cent and return on equity (RoE) of 13.7 per cent by FY28.
 Reported NIM improved 50 bps Q-o-Q to 9.52 per cent, due to utilisation of equity infusion proceeds received from Japan’s MUFG on account of a stake purchase by the latter. Yields as calculated declined 10 bps Q-o-Q to 16.65 per cent while cost of borrowing as calculated declined 15 bps Q-o-Q to 8.47 per cent. The spread was 8.18 per cent as compared to 8.15 per cent in Q1FY27. The shift in the rate cycle following the hike in Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) latest monetary policy makes earlier expectations of 100 bps reduction in cost of funds unlikely.
 Management expects NIM to remain broadly stable at current levels over the next two quarters, before moderating to 9 per cent in FY28 and 8.5 per cent longer-term. The FY26 NIM was 8.2 per cent.
 The market was spooked by rising credit costs. Gross Stage 3 (GS3) and Net Stage 3 (NS3) were held at 4.65 per cent and 2.3 per cent, respectively. Net slippages increased 12 bps Q-o-Q to 2.06 per cent (Q2FY26 was 1.6 per cent and Q12FY27 was 1.93 per cent). Stage 2 assets rose 10 bps Q-o-Q to 7.05 per cent from 6.95 per cent Q-o-Q and 6.9 per cent Y-o-Y. Write-offs amounted to 1.1 per cent of trailing 12 month AUM, of about ₹800 crore. The Stage 2 stress was visible in 2W, CVs, MSME, tractors, and gold loans. Stage 3 also rose in 2W, gold and personal loans.
 The management said that monsoon stress has hurt production of rice, soybean, maize, cotton, and pulses, and West Asia tensions have led to fertiliser shortages. This is affecting rural consumption demand. The company is trying to diversify the rural portfolio into coverage of non-farm activities.
 The lowering of AUM guidance and warnings about continued elevated credit costs have already resulted in a correction. Long-term credit cost guidance stays at 2 per cent, implying credit cost normalisation in FY28. Shriram Finance looks to double the gold loan portfolio over three years, increasing share of AUM to 5 per cent. MSME growth will accelerate but the segment has 28 per cent unsecured loans with stress concentrated in drought-affected regions. The proposed Irdai draft guidelines may result in reduction of insurance commission income by up to ₹100 crore (₹350 crore in insurance commissions was received in FY26).
 While analysts have reduced target prices and downgraded earnings, many remain positive on the stock which trades at moderate valuations. According to Bloomberg, 35 of 36 analysts polled post results are bullish. Their average one-year target price is ₹1,129.

docs.title: 9 ‘Buy’ recommendations by Motilal Oswal with 21% to 34% upside potential
docs.text: Motilal Oswal has reiterated ‘Buy’ ratings on nine stocks across sectors, including chemicals, quick commerce, cables, asset management and real estate, with target prices indicating potential upside of 21% to 34%. According to the brokerage report dated October 22, the investment cases vary. Some companies could benefit from capacity expansion and improving demand, while others need to address margin pressures, rising costs or persistent losses. Here is a look at Motilal Oswal’s nine stock recommendations, their target prices and the factors behind each call. Motilal Oswal on SRF Motilal Oswal has set a target price of Rs 3,000 for SRF, indicating an upside of 28%. According to the brokerage report, earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) grew 30% year-on-year in the Q2FY27. However, higher raw material and logistics costs weighed on margins. The brokerage expects growth to receive support from refrigerant gases, fluoropolymers and the performance films and foil business. It said, “We expect SRF to maintain the growth momentum in FY27”. The recovery in specialty chemicals and the ramp-up of new capacities will remain important factors to watch. ALSO READNarayana Murthy’s family office bets Rs 310 cr on 2 new, beaten-down stocks Motilal Oswal on Swiggy Swiggy has a target price of Rs 280, implying an upside of 32%. According to Motilal Oswal, revenue grew 36.7% year-on-year in the first half of FY27, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) losses narrowed to Rs 1,400 crore from Rs 1,500 crore a year earlier. However, the brokerage expects losses to rise in the second half. Instamart's slower growth and competition from rivals such as Blinkit remain concerns. Motilal Oswal said, “a clear path toward QC EBITDA profitability remains critical for a meaningful re-rating.” Motilal Oswal on KEI Industries Motilal Oswal has a target price of Rs 5,180 for KEI Industries, suggesting a 34% upside. The brokerage has reduced its target from Rs 5,670 after trimming its earnings estimates. Management expects revenue growth of around 25% in FY27, but margins and the execution of capacity expansion remain key monitorables. Motilal Oswal on RR Kabel For R R Kabel, the brokerage has set a target price of Rs 2,960, implying a 30% upside. Its investment case rests on expanding cable operations, exports and improving profitability. Motilal Oswal expects revenue, EBITDA and profit after tax to grow at compound annual growth rates (CAGR) of approximately 25%, 36% and 40%, respectively, between FY26 and FY28. Motilal Oswal on Nippon Life India AMC Nippon Life India Asset Management has a target price of Rs 1,200, indicating a 24% upside. According to the report, its retail business, systematic investment plan (SIP) flows and digital expansion could support growth. However, the brokerage has cut its FY27 and FY28 earnings estimates by 4% and 1%, respectively, partly because of a settlement fee. ALSO READBrokerage consensus stocks: Swiggy, Eternal among 6 stock picks with 22% to 91% upside Motilal Oswal on Sagility Sagility has a target price of Rs 57, implying a 25% upside. Motilal Oswal expects the healthcare services company to benefit from additional work from existing clients, new client additions, cross-selling and acquisition-related synergies. Motilal Oswal on CreditAccess Grameen Motilal Oswal sees a 33% upside in CreditAccess Grameen, with a target price of Rs 1,450. The brokerage expects growth in assets under management (AUM) and improving profitability to support its outlook, although weather-related disruptions and credit costs warrant monitoring. Motilal Oswal on CIE Automotive CIE Automotive India has a target price of Rs 440, indicating a 21% upside. The brokerage expects its Indian operations to benefit from improving demand and new order wins, while its European business continues to focus on margins. Motilal Oswal on Mahindra Lifespaces Mahindra Lifespaces rounds out the list with a target price of Rs 470 and a potential upside of 34%. The brokerage added, "We maintain our presales CAGR estimate of 27% to reach Rs 5,460 crore during FY26-28." The brokerage’s preferred picks include companies expanding their project pipelines, strengthening cash generation, improving operating performance or benefiting from favourable industry conditions. Godrej Properties and Adani Energy Solutions feature prominently on the list, supported by expectations of stronger cash flows and sustained earnings growth. JK Cement’s capacity expansion plans and IndusInd Bank’s potential profitability recovery also support Jefferies’ view. For Bharat Petroleum Corporation, refining performance remains a key earnings driver, while Au Small Finance Bank’s growing deposit franchise and transition to a universal bank form important parts of its investment case. Jefferies on Godrej Properties: 'Buy' Jefferies has a 'Buy' on Godrej Properties, with a target price of Rs 2,550, implying an upside potential of 63%. In its October 23 report, the brokerage pointed to improved collections, stronger operating cash generation and a healthy project launch pipeline. Collections rose 31% year on year in the September quarter, while the operating cash flow surplus more than doubled. Jefferies sees scope for stronger pre-sales in the second half of FY27 as new projects come to market. The company’s management raised its FY27 pre-sales guidance to Rs 39,200 crore to Rs 41,700 crore, implying growth of 15% to 22% year on year. Jefferies expects stronger cash generation to support positive free cash flow in the second half of FY27 and through FY28. It also considers management’s FY28 target of a 20% reported return on equity achievable. The brokerage’s assessment rests on the company’s ability to convert its project pipeline into sales and cash collections, while maintaining growth over the coming financial years. “Strong launch pipeline near term could drive a guidance beat taking pre-sales growth to 20%+,” Jefferies said. Jefferies on Adani Energy Solutions: 'Buy' Jefferies has a 'Buy' on Adani Energy Solutions, with a target price of Rs 1,980, implying an upside potential of 62%. In its October 25 report, the brokerage said the company’s September-quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) exceeded expectations, led by its trading business. Jefferies raised its FY27 EBITDA estimate by 6%, although it trimmed estimates for FY28 to FY30 to account for lower expected capitalisation in transmission and smart meters. The trading segment has become a more significant contributor to earnings. Jefferies also pointed to the company’s renewable energy and battery energy storage capacity tie-ups as potential support for the business. Meanwhile, its transmission project pipeline offers another source of expansion, with projects worth Rs 87,200 crore under execution. Although the brokerage lowered its transmission capitalisation expectations for FY27 and FY28, it remained positive on the company’s longer-term growth prospects. Higher sales volumes supported the performance, although rising fuel and other operating costs weighed on profitability per tonne. Standalone grey and white cement volumes increased 21% and 14% year on year, respectively. Jefferies noted that cost pressures could persist into the following quarter, while cement price increases introduced across the industry in October could offer some relief. The company’s capacity expansion programme remains central to its longer-term plans. The North India expansion is expected to take cement capacity to around 40 million tonnes per annum in the first half of FY28. Further brownfield projects are intended to support its target of reaching 50 million tonnes of capacity by FY30. Jefferies also noted progress in JK Cement’s adjacent businesses, including wall putty and water-based paints. Its investment case rests on volume growth, planned capacity additions and the company’s ability to manage operating costs as it expands. In its October 23 report, the brokerage said the bank’s September-quarter profit was ahead of expectations, supported by lower credit costs and stronger fee and treasury income. docs.title: Shriram Finance falls 6%: Brokerages see up to 40% upside on portfolio diversification
docs.text: The Shriram Finance share price plunged over 6% on Monday, October 26. The management flagged concerns of rising credit costs due to a weaker monsoon and also lowered the full year growth guidance. However, global investment bank Jefferies and brokerages Motilal Oswal and Nuvama have maintained their respective ‘Buy’ rating on the stock. Shriram Finance Q2 earnings Shriram Finance on Friday reported a 59% rise in consolidated net profit for the September quarter to Rs 3,683.81 crore, from Rs 2,314.16 crore a year earlier. Total income rose 15.8% to Rs 13,801.84 crore in the quarter. Interest income, the largest component, grew 15.9% to Rs 13,385.84 crore. Jefferies on Shriram Finance: Rising stress in drought-hit states The global investment bank has maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock, but lowered its price target by 5% to Rs 1,145 apiece. This implies an upside of nearly 39% from the stock’s current price of Rs 824.95. Jefferies has raised its FY27 earnings per share (EPS) estimate by 2%, factoring in better net interest margin (NIM), lower opex, and higher credit costs. However, it has cut the FY28-FY29 EPS on lower NIMs, fee income, and lower credit costs. “We expect EPS to grow at 15% EPS CAGR over FY26-28 and ROE inching up to 14% by FY28e (13.3% FY27e).” ALSO READMonday Watchlist: Nifty volatility spikes — IT, Pharma & Realty among key sectors to watch Jefferies expects assets under management (AUM) to grow 17%/18% in FY27-FY28. Growth was noted in CV AUMs, gold loans, personal loans, and micro, small, and medium enterprise loans. Broader demand is healthy but Shriram Fin’s management flagged rising stress in drought-hit states like Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, after a weak monsoon. “SHFL has tightened lending in these regions, and is guiding for 16-17% AUM growth (18-20% earlier).” Jefferies expects NIMs to be resilient in the near term, and the impact of fee income should be lower than peers. Motilal Oswal on Shriram Finance: Maintains ‘Buy’ with 40% upside Domestic brokerage firm Motilal Oswal also reiterated its ‘Buy’ call on the stock, and has a target price of Rs 1,155. This implies an upside of 40% from the current price. “SHFL delivered a mixed quarter, with PPoP beating estimates on the back of higher NIM and lower opex, while earnings were in line owing to higher credit costs. AUM growth at 17% YoY was stronger than our estimate; however, credit costs increased amid higher slippages and write-offs, primarily reflecting drought-like conditions across multiple states in India. Hence, management raised its FY27 credit cost guidance and lowered its AUM growth outlook,” the brokerage said. The company indicated that credit costs could rise temporarily by 30-40 bps over the next one or two quarters due to seasonal stress in affected geographies. Weak monsoons are weighing on rural consumption, particularly entry-level two-wheelers and cars, discretionary FMCG, and consumer appliances. However, diversification into non-farm and allied activities, greater irrigation coverage, and lower rainfall dependence have improved rural resilience. Nuvama on Shriram Finance: Strong growth, margin to absorb high provisions Nuvama retained its ‘Buy’ recommendation on the stock with a target price of Rs 1,150 apiece, implying an upside of 39%. “We forecast Shriram’s strong growth and margin momentum shall help absorb elevated provisions while sustaining more than 4% RoA/13–15% RoE over FY27–29E. However, rising rural stress and sector-wide valuation de-rating (as CoE rise) warrant a cut in target multiple for Shriram too,” Nuvama said. ALSO READBrokerage consensus stocks: Swiggy, Eternal among 6 stock picks with 22% to 91% upside While the shift towards new vehicle financing could dilute yields by 200–400bp against used vehicles, MSME expansion and the plan to double gold loans’ share of AUM to 5% over three years should support portfolio diversification and also yields, the brokerage added. Shriram Finance: What investors should watch next? The company has flagged concerns about rural consumption and weak monsoon increasing credit costs. Any progress in demand will be closely monitored as brokerages predict firm AUM growth amid portfolio diversification.
